en: Preface to the *Heart Sūtra* Exegesis Dispelling Doubts.
Master Mo Hu was a native of Min who harbored ambitions as vast as the universe.

Admiring the character of Sima Qian, he traveled across half the empire, internalizing within his breast all the famous mountains and great rivers he encountered during his journey. It was while traveling through Zhejiang that he composed this work.
He traveled up to Kuaiji, exploring the Cave of Yu until he arrived at Wulin.

Wulin was indeed a great metropolis where those of manifold wisdom and eloquence from all quarters gathered with the various schools of thought and diverse arts; there they displayed their talents and vied for preeminence.
Yet Mo Hu was only dull and stammering, as if entirely incapable of anything. His spirit was refreshingly clear, and his appearance was emaciated.

Anciently, his mind was profoundly sincere and earnest; was he not indeed a man of the Way? When questioned, he was broadly versed in both ancient and modern matters, and there were no profound mysteries of the imperial canon or Buddhist scriptures that he had not investigated.
He was particularly adept in the discourse of geomancy (*kānyú*), for he followed it entirely according to the *I Ching*.

Thus, the topography and strategic advantages of the land were as clear to him as looking at the palm of his hand. He once said of himself: "The *I Ching* is the calculation of reversals; [it is the same principle as] Fengshui."

As for the Way of the Golden Elixir (*Jindan*), how could it be anything other than "reversal" (*ni*)? Nevertheless, it still lags behind the physical body and ultimately returns to the realm of illusion and transformation;
it is not equal to the transcendence of the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) by the "Formless One," who ascends directly to the other shore.
Among his writings, there is a commentary on the *Heart Sūtra*, yet its meaning remains incomplete. He also composed various treatises resolving doubts, such as the *Huh* (Calling Out).
It is to cause those who are asleep to awaken. Even the most ignorant men and women can know how to become Buddhas and Patriarchs;

by following these words, one may enter [the Way]. Furthermore, those in the world who revile the Buddha say: "The Buddha taught that the mind is non-existent. How can the mind be said to be non-existent? Master Mo Hu replied:
"To be free from all deluded minds is precisely what it means for the Buddha to have no mind. Again, those who revile the Buddhist teachings say: "There is a substance..."
It is useless. How could one know the subtlety that form and emptiness are not different? Nor is this apart from worldly dharmas.

If one were to seek bodhi by departing from the world, could such a person even be mentioned in the same breath as this? By clearing away the brambles of the Buddhist path, this serves as a guiding compass for future students.
His achievements in the Gate of Emptiness are by no means a minor contribution. Having completed my study of this book, I regret that I am unable to attain the realization of Śūnyatā-jāti;
nevertheless, I have composed this preface in response to the request of the shaven-headed monk and the official Hu Shijun.

Written on a spring day in the Dinghai year of the Wanli era by Xu Yue of Qiantang, a former jinshi, while adrift in a raft upon the waters of the Qiong Sea. Explanations for Doubts Regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* composed by the Daoist of Jianyi in Min, the "One-Cap" practitioner, Hehu Xie Ziguan. [Exegesis] The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* is the essence of the Great Vehicle’s profound wisdom. It is the ultimate destination of all Buddhas and the source of all sages. Its meaning is vast and its principles are subtle; it is difficult to fathom and easy to err. Therefore, I have compiled these notes to clarify the text and resolve doubts, hoping that those who encounter this scripture will not be led astray. First, regarding the title: "Prajñāpāramitā" is translated as "Perfection of Wisdom. "Hṛdaya" is translated as "Heart" or "Essence. "Sūtra" is translated as "Discourse. Together, they signify the core of the Great Perfection of Wisdom. Second, regarding the opening invocation: "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" refers to the Great Compassionate One who observes the world. "Mahāsattva" means a great being. "Coursing in the deep Prajñāpāramitā" means practicing the profound perfection of wisdom. "Illuminated and perceived" refers to his clear and unhindered insight. "All the five aggregates" refers to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "Seen to be empty" means realizing their lack of inherent self-nature. "Relieved from all suffering and distress" means attaining liberation through the cessation of delusion. Third, regarding the Buddha's response: "At that time, the Bhagavat" refers to the World-Honored One. "Was dwelling in Śrāvastī" indicates his location. "In the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada" specifies the setting. "With a great assembly of bhikṣus" describes the gathering of monastics. "At that time, the Bhagavat entered the samādhi called 'Profoundly Observing the Profundities of the Dharmadhātu'" indicates the Buddha’s meditative state. "And simultaneously entered the lion’s roar" signifies his majestic power. "The bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara... spoke these words to the Buddha" records the transmission of the teaching. Fourth, regarding the core teaching: "Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Vulture Peak Cave, with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. This is the prologue. "At that time, the Bhagavat entered the samādhi called 'Profoundly Observing the Profundities of the Dharmadhātu. This establishes the context. "Then the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: 'O Bhagavat, how should a son of good family train in the profound Prajñāpāramitā? This is the inquiry. "The Buddha told Śāriputra: 'If a son of good family wishes to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he should perceive all phenomena as empty of self-nature. This is the answer. "There is no birth, no extinction, no defilement, no purity, no increase, and no decrease. This explains the nature of emptiness. "Because there is no form, there is no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. This negates the five aggregates. "Because there is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind," and so forth, up to "no ignorance and no end of ignorance," and "no old age and death and no end of old age and death. This negates the eighteen elements and the twelve links of dependent origination. "No suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path. This negates the Four Noble Truths. "No wisdom and no attainment. This negates the fruits of the path. "Therefore, in the Prajñāpāramitā, there is nothing to attain. This concludes the teaching. Fifth, regarding the conclusion: "When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the venerable Śāriputra and the entire great assembly, as well as the gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. This records the response and the dissemination of the teaching. This work is intended to aid students in understanding the text and to prevent misinterpretation. May it serve as a lamp for the Dharma-eye. The monk Liaohan of Qiantang, formerly a Jinshi (Metropolitan Graduate), and Hu Xiao have collated and examined this.
Regarding "Avalokiteśvara," the commentaries of various schools all take "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" as a single phrase; for instance, Zongle’s commentary takes "Avalokite... [and so forth].
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara answered Śāriputra’s question. He visited the assemblies of all the Buddhas, yet found no bodhisattva named Avalokiteśvara.
Only the Bodhisattva Guanyin existed; his original name was Miaoyin, and he was in male form.
He was an attendant to the Tathāgata Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (Sukhāvatī-vyūha-lokadhātu) in the Eastern World of Pure Radiance Adornment, having received his teacher’s command.
I have come to this Sahā world to inquire after the well-being of our Buddha, to behold the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, and to hear the wondrous sound of the Lotus Sūtra.
Having fulfilled all subtle practices, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati offered me a jeweled necklace as an act of worship;

yet, having not yet received the Buddha’s instruction, I did not dare accept it. How could I, following the Buddha’s command, presume to overstep my station? This is the great occasion for preaching the Dharma.
It is so. The *Sūtra of the Universal Gate* (*Pumen jing*) is likewise; it was spoken by the World-Honored One to the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati.
It can be known that this "Avalokiteśvara" is certainly not a name for a bodhisattva. Furthermore, there is no basis for [the claim] that Śāriputra inquired on behalf of the assembly.
Alas, because the tradition has been practiced for so long and its essential meaning has not been clearly realized, one suddenly fails to [understand] the three characters "Guān-zì-zài."
Pay heed! To allow the Buddha’s profound teachings to remain obscured for a thousand or ten thousand generations is truly a matter of deep lamentation.

I have devoted my heart and mind to the sutras for over twenty years; I have come to realize that the wondrous essence of these sutras lies in Prajñāpāramitā. Prajñā is precisely the contemplation of Avalokiteśvara.
World-Honored One, it is like a king of physicians who takes the single character "contemplation" (guan) as the gateway to sagehood, thereby dispensing the wondrous medicine.
It cures the diseases of all afflictions for sentient beings; if one has faith and takes it, the effect of attaining mastery will surely be realized.
Generally speaking, the Buddha-dharma takes the deconstruction of appearances as its core principle and the realization of emptiness as its meaning.

Yet, as for this contemplation, what else could there be apart from the relinquishing of the body? It is, in fact, a method of borrowing the provisional to cultivate the real. Were it not for this body, the mind would have no basis.

Appendix: By means of what does one practice? It is simply because the World-Honored One feared that sentient beings would become attached to this body—preferring life and loathing death—that he pointed out it to be an illusory and transformative thing, composed of the combination of earth, water, fire, and wind.
Prior to birth, one was enticed by hunger, cold, and sensual desires, thereby falsely creating karma such as greed and anger; for this reason, one is unable to escape the cycle of the three realms.
The suffering of saṃsāra. Yet this illusory body ultimately returns to decay; only the true nature of the spirit exists eternally from antiquity.
That which people ought to know and clarify is that they turn their backs on daily life and do not recognize the Buddha. Therefore, this teaching of the destruction of marks was spoken;
though words do not reach the body, the body is already contained within them. Those of the Buddhist tradition today have misunderstood it...

They often feel revulsion toward this body, claiming that without this physical frame, there would be no afflictions. Such people have already fallen into the deep pit of the nihilistic view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*);
thus, the School of Mystery (*xuanmen*) mocks them as "the solitary souls of those who have lost their masters.

How is it that the School of Mystery does not clarify the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), but from the very start becomes mired in the physical shell? Furthermore, they have yielded the primacy of the mind and fundamental nature to the Chan school.
Such people are numerous. How could they know that one must accumulate essence and gather vital energy to establish the foundation and refine the self?

If one does not understand one's original nature, one will be driven at every turn by deluded thoughts and enticed by illusory phenomena. Consequently, because these thoughts do not cease, the mind is not at peace;

because the spirit does not coalesce, the vital energy does not gather. If the vital energy does not gather, the elixir cannot be perfected; how then can one hope to reach the spine and the double-barrier?
Is there truly such a thing as a creator? These people have already fallen into the snare of the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

The Buddha once rebuked them as non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and Zen practitioners mock them as "hungry ghosts guarding corpses. Therefore, Master Ziyang said: "Before refining the cinnabar elixir, first refine one's nature;
before cultivating the great medicine, first cultivate the mind. When the mind is still, the elixir is naturally attained; when the nature is pure, the elixir is perfected."
Only then is the medicinal prescription perfected; it has never been anything other than using the study of the nature of mind to remedy the loss of partiality and deficiency.
The illness of these two streams is, in its essence, one and the same.

If one were to awaken to Avalokiteśvara or practice the dharma-gate of the profound Prajñāpāramitā, how could such an illness exist? This contemplation is the contemplation of that which is without anything to be contemplated.
This is not the contemplation of turning the light back upon itself to reflect. For as soon as one fixes upon "turning back," there is already a location.
Once there is a location, there is internally a mind that knows and externally an object that is seen. When mind and object are set in opposition, the practice is easily interrupted;
one becomes unable to bear the exhaustion. How, then, could the effect of self-mastery be attained? Or perhaps...
To falsely point to the various apertures and cavities within the body and observe them is to suffer from the dualistic affliction of subject and object;

none of these constitute the correct and sublime contemplation. Only the Great Contemplation exists, which has no cause and no beginning. Thus, one attains freedom in both going and staying, moving with ease and clarity in all directions.
Though it is said that there is nothing, this does not mean being obstructed by any objects or phenomena.
Who does not know that there is, of itself, that which cannot be dispelled? It arises unflinchingly, becoming the abiding place of true, great, and correct reality.

For those who transcend the world, when this true object of contemplation exists, the mind first becomes settled, desire first becomes empty, the body first becomes clear, and the mind first becomes still.

When the body is empty and the mind is still, the wondrous state of lightness and ease is attained spontaneously without seeking; it is the realm of the true mark (*dharmatā*), realized of itself without being proven.
Thus it is called the "Treasure Place" (*ratnasthāna*). One who is able to dwell in this place will find that all external conditions and phenomena revolve around them like the stars in the heavens;
this is the essence of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Now, although external conditions are provisional, they cannot fail to respond.
If one responds to them without forgetting their proper place, then things will manifest their true nature. Things remain as things and cannot disturb me.
Compared to this truth, those who turn their backs on conditions and simplify their affairs fall far behind. This is the function of contemplation (*guan*).
If objects have nothing for the mind to respond to, then emotional consciousness (*qing-shi*) arises. Once emotional consciousness has formed, one mistakes objects for reality.
To mistake objects for reality is to have the fires of desire blaze together and the afflictions of the world swarm forth; thus, there is no longer the subtlety of contemplating objects.
Yet, when one contemplates its essence and function, both are lost. This contemplation herein takes the mountains and rivers of the entire earth as the single eye of the śramaṇa;

it is the grand contemplation that encompasses both the internal and external. One who possesses this contemplation fuses the six sense organs and six sense objects into one great perfect penetration (*ekāntara-samāpatti*), and transforms earth, water, fire, and wind into the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the realm of clarity. This is precisely what is meant by "a single grain of divine elixir."
To turn base metal into gold with a single word of the Ultimate Way is to transform the mundane into the sacred.

One who contemplates in this manner realizes the identity of essence and function, thereby attaining for the first time the path of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is empty, true, sovereign, and perfectly complete.
When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, "bodhi" means awakening;

this is translated as "enlightenment," which is the Buddha. "Sattva" means a sentient being (*sattva*); this is translated as "sentient beings" who possess consciousness, which refers to living beings.
To speak in detail, it is called *bodhisattva*; to speak briefly, it is called "bodhisattva. This is translated as:
This refers to the sentient being who is awakened. Now, the awakened nature of sentient beings is no different from that of a Buddha;

however, since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have been defiled by the habitual tendencies of all emotional consciousnesses, which have clouded the nature of perfect awakening and transformed it into deluded thoughts. Because of these discursive thoughts...

Life arises incessantly; therefore, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). The Buddha specifically refers to them as "Awakened Ones" (*buddha*), because their awakened nature (*bodhi*) is perfectly luminous, pure and singular without artifice, and has utterly severed all emotional consciousness (*saṃjñā-vijñāna*).
Although they possess emotional consciousness, it is entirely transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*).
Its radiance shines universally, like the bright sun in the midst of the sky, eternally without change. It is for this reason alone that the Buddha is uniquely termed "the Awakened. Indeed.

The Bodhisattva stands between the Buddha and sentient beings, between the ordinary and the sagely. Why is this? Although they possess right enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), their awakening is not yet complete;
they still harbor subtle emotional consciousness that has not been entirely purified.

Therefore, they are called "enlightened sentient beings" (*bodhisattva*). As Prime Minister Pei said: "Those who are perfectly enlightened all day long, yet have never experienced perfect enlightenment, are ordinary beings."

Furthermore, those who are fully endowed with perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) and abide in the maintenance of perfect enlightenment are Tathāgatas. Those who wish to realize perfect enlightenment but have not yet reached its ultimate consummation are Bodhisattvas.
Now, the perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is identical in every respect.

However, the emotional consciousnesses of sentient beings within the triple world are diverse for each individual, and the knowledge and views of the Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions vary in their degrees of magnitude.

Therefore, they are divided into eleven stages (*bhūmi*). The Bodhisattva of the first stage perceives the luminosity of the awakened nature (*bodhicitta*) as a single thread briefly revealed, like the crescent moon at the beginning of spring;
this is named the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because one has realized the state of a sage (*ārya*).

The Bodhisattva of the second stage is named the Stage Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), like the fourth day of the new moon, signifying that their body and mind have become pure. The Bodhisattva of the third stage...

*Sā*. Like the moonlight on the first day of the sixth lunar phase, it is even greater; because its great wisdom has already become luminous, it is named the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

The Bodhisattva of the fourth ground possesses a wondrous understanding that shines forth universally, resembling the moon on the first day of the seventh lunar phase; as wisdom gradually becomes manifest, it is named the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
The Bodhisattva of the fifth ground penetrates both the ultimate and conventional truths, and is thus named the Ground of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*). And...
Its radiance is like that of the crescent moon on the first half of the month. The knowledge and vision of a Bodhisattva in the sixth stage is like the moon of the tenth day;
its brightness exceeds that of the crescent because its meritorious practice transcends all others, and thus it is named the "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā) Stage.

A Bodhisattva in the seventh stage possesses the capacity to manifest transformations according to various directions, and thus it is named the "Far-Reaching" (Dūraṃgamā) Stage, like the moon on the eleventh night.
It is like the moon. In the eighth stage, where patience and wisdom are as one's will, it is called the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

In the ninth stage, the Bodhisattva possesses mastery over supernormal powers; like the moonlight on the thirteenth night, it is full yet not yet complete, and is called the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
The tenth stage: Great wisdom is perfectly luminous and covers all things; it is named the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*). It is like the moon on the fourteenth day;
although its light is full, it has not yet reached the full moon. This Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is like Kāśyapa and others within the assembly of the Buddha.
Furthermore, their knowledge and vision do not equal that of the great bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
whose radiance is universally pervasive, without deficiency or remainder, like the moon on the fifteenth day.

This gradation of superiority and inferiority among the bodhisattvas of the eleventh stage exists solely because the power of their supernatural penetrations (*abhijñā*) and their *dharmas* differ in magnitude.
Although all sentient beings within the three realms may be noble or base, wise or foolish, their knowledge and vision are entirely obscured by emotional consciousness and arrogance;
thus they block the luminosity of their own nature, which is like the waning of the moon. Their entire being becomes dark and obscure, as if they were blind.
Consequently, when they encounter objects, they become instantly "sticky" and all turns into affliction. Alas! It is truly a pity that they do not get to hear the Buddha-dharma.
It is said that those for whom the ten thousand ages are like a long night are such people.
Yet, if all sentient beings can practice the profound Dharma of Prajñā, they may likewise proceed from the shore of the first bhūmi to the nirvāṇa of the eleventh bhūmi.
Now, Prajñāpāramitā has both shallow and deep aspects. The shallow refers to the śrāvakas, who are only able to empty the discursive thoughts within their minds;
they do not dare to respond to external objects, for if they were to respond, they would inevitably be obstructed by the dharmas that serve as sensory objects.

They possess only the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā-prajñā). The deep aspect is the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā-prajñā), which only those who cultivate the bodhisattva path are capable of attaining. This is because...
Not only does it empty the mind of all internal afflictions, but it also illuminates and perceives that all external things and objects—the phenomena of worldly toil—are entirely empty.
Therefore, it is called the wisdom of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmāśūnyatā-prajñā*). One who practices this profound *prajñā* has a mind-ground that is brilliantly clear.
Sentimental views are thus dissolved like ice. Dwelling amidst the mundane, one does not cling to existence; departing from the mundane, one does not cling to emptiness.
A person such as this has only then attained profound *prajñā*. *Prajñā* is simply the recognition of phenomena so that one is not bound by them; this is itself wisdom.
Now, the worldly fame, profit, and sensual desires constitute many demonic realms; without *prajñā*, none can overcome them.
To shatter [the mind], nothing surpasses the head of this army: female beauty. Behold those exquisite forms and seductive postures—what differ they from long spears and short arrows?
Those cloud-like tresses and misty locks are just like lassos and flying clubs; those autumnal glances are like iron shooting stars; that scarlet peach-like mouth is like a hair-piercing blade;
and those wondrous teeth, with their faint, mocking smiles, cause the foolish man’s soul to scatter and his spirit to vanish. The feet of this demon...
Stealthily and unsteadily they sway; the hero’s heart is anxious and his courage falters.

Upon investigating the cause of this loss of virtue and the ruin of his will, he finds it lies solely in his love for the charms of skin and flesh, unaware that he has already fallen into the trap of seductive beauty. Can this be called wisdom?
If one possessed the eye of profound *prajñā*, one would see through the skin, hair, claws, teeth, viscera, sinews, bones, vital energy, blood, and essence.
Tsin. Present each item individually and examine them closely. Which among them possesses the power to move the heart?
Whenever you encounter a person or a thing, use this method of breaking through appearances (*lakṣaṇa-bhañjana*) to analyze and observe them.

Only when you have discerned and seen through their various artificial adornments and combinations does one attain the profound *prajñā* of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Even after a hundred years have passed since your death, that—
All these are but people within a dream or an illusion. Why, then, do you remain deluded before your very eyes, lingering in attachment to defile and burden yourself?
This Prajñāpāramitā that shatters appearances may at first require effort, but after a long time it becomes natural. To be deluded is to be caught in the endless cycle of birth and death;
to awaken is to ascend directly to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Its subtlety lies in practice; without practice, one cannot reach the other shore. [The character for] "practice" (行).
This is the "eye of the sūtra" for this section. A proverb says: "If you can walk one step having realized it, it is a waste not to walk that one step.
One must understand that speaking of knowing Chang'an and actually walking there cannot be conflated. The ancients used "knowing" as a metaphor for the eyes and "walking" as a metaphor for the feet.
To have eyes but no feet is to fail to reach the other shore; to have feet but no eyes is not to know where one is going.
Now that you have understood through Prajñā, if you are willing to put it into practice, you will attain it immediately—this is the swift efficacy of the emptiness of the five aggregates.
"To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty:
while Prajñā indeed resides in practice, the five aggregates reside in perception. Without perception, the five aggregates are not empty."

The single character "Illumination" (zhào) is the eye through which one exerts effort in this section. The five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are also called the five *skandhas*.
*Skandha* carries the meaning of "covering" or "obscuring," as well as the meaning of "accumulation. They constantly enshroud and entangle the human mind.
The karma of greed and hatred constitutes the successive stages of the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*), not the five physical locations.

The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is the collective name for the six external sense-objects. The four aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness constitute the successive stages of the deluded mind.
If a person can first recognize the forms of the six external sense-objects and refuse to accept them, then even form will be unable [to bind them].
This constitutes the aggregate of mind. If one applies diligent effort within the state of non-reception (*anupādāna*), it is the most effortless method;
then the six external sense-objects and the six internal consciousnesses will immediately collapse at both ends. Only those who are truly diligent can constantly attain this bliss.
As for the indolent person, the mind merges with the sense-objects; because the mind merges with the objects, form is already received by the mind.

Therefore, feeling (*vedanā*) constitutes the second aggregate (*skandha*). When one does not forget that feeling, there arises perception (*saṃjñā*); at the moment of perceiving, one has already entered the third aggregate.

When perception continues unabated, there arise mental formations (*saṃskāra*); with these formations, one has already entered the fourth aggregate. Through these formations, one recognizes the significance of the object; this aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the fifth.
Once form has entered deeply into the mind, consciousness becomes difficult to forget. As sensory contact arises again, the Sūtra says: "Even if..."
"Even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the karma one has created is not forgotten; when the causes and conditions meet, one must again experience the retribution oneself.
This refers to what the Buddha meant when he said that this body of the five aggregates has consciousness as its root, and further stated that consciousness is the seed of birth and death.
If one can illuminate and penetrate through form, then the root of consciousness will finally be severed and the source of awakening will finally become clear.

Some may suspect that the five aggregates are all empty, believing that body, mind, and external phenomena ultimately revert to illusion and transformation, concluding that in the end they are all but a single emptiness;
thus, they fix their minds upon this state of emptiness, gripping it firmly, striving to make the mind like extinguished ashes.
They possess no wisdom or insight whatsoever, yet they claim to have attained something. The Buddha rebuked such people as having incurable illnesses;

they do not contemplate liberation from the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and furthermore, they become attached to this emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Yet even this emptiness is itself one aggregate. Yongjia said:
"To abandon existence and cling to non-existence is likewise an illness; it is like avoiding drowning by throwing oneself into fire. The Sixth Patriarch said: "First of all, do not be attached."
"Emptiness. Furthermore, it is said: "There are those who delude themselves, sitting in meditation with an empty mind and no thoughts at all, yet claiming for themselves to be great.
Because such deluded people hold false views, one should not speak with them. This 'emptiness' of the emptiness of the five aggregates has caused many to fall into ruin.
Those whose awakening is not genuine cling to their minds in a state of folly; they are as rare as those who do not die from ingesting aconite poison. Great!

Most later students fall into this pitfall; the Buddha once rebuked them, saying they were practitioners of the Two Vehicles. However, this emptiness is extremely difficult to describe. I would liken it to a bottle:
when water is poured into it, it is called a "water-bottle"; when tea is poured into it, it is called a "tea-bottle.
If there is neither water nor tea, it is called an "empty bottle. Although it is called an "empty bottle," this merely means that there is nothing inside the bottle.
It is not that the jar itself is non-existent. In the same way, within the true mind of a person there are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);

these are called the "deluded mind. When they are absent, it is called the "empty mind. Although it is said that the mind is empty, this merely means that the five aggregates are absent within the mind;
it does not mean that the mind itself is non-existent. What the Buddhist tradition refers to as "no-mind" (*acitta*) is the absence of all deluded thoughts; it is not the absence of the mind itself.
When conceptual thought ceases, the true mind appears before one. However, those whose entry into the gate is shallow cannot see it suddenly;
they must undergo refinement over a long period before they can attain sudden enlightenment.
There are teachers of this sort who, having departed from the five aggregates and yet not clinging to emptiness, remain suspended in the void.

Between existence and emptiness, they claim for themselves that they do not cling to existence externally nor cling to emptiness internally, asserting that they have realized the Middle Way. Alas, these people are already exhausted;
do not cling to the sickness of the "Middle. Once the five aggregates are understood as empty, there must necessarily be a true reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) before it is possible.
Otherwise, there would be no basis for establishing destiny as a secret place of reclusion.
Though this class of people may possess the talent to ascend the clouds and walk upon the moon, they will ultimately find it difficult to escape this latent storehouse—the cycle of birth and death.
The Buddha and sentient beings are similar in body and mind; their knowledge and vision are no different, their five aggregates are identical, and their eating and drinking are not distinct.
Yet, within these five aggregates, sentient beings follow after external objects and undergo constant flux, repeatedly deluded by views and afflictions, thereby constructing the causes for the hells.

It is not that they do not feel weary of and seek to leave [suffering], but because they do not know that the aggregates belong to themselves, from infancy until old age, they identify with the aggregates.
This is indeed true. For phenomena arise through mutual conditioning and habitual association, evolving together with them.

Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, regarding these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), remain unstained by the current while performing the Buddha-work of precepts, concentration, and wisdom within those very aggregates. Therefore, they neither weary of nor abandon them, for they cannot abandon them.
Where there is this mind, there must necessarily be the five aggregates; it is like a fish that cannot leave the water. To leave the water—
He died immediately. A tiger cannot leave the mountain; if it leaves the mountain, it is captured. My mind’s reliance upon the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is just like this.
The five aggregates are indeed unpleasant things, yet even a Buddha cannot be without them. However, for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...

When one’s knowledge and vision are upright and great, they all transform into virtuous qualities and noble conduct; one undergoes transformation along with them. The Sixth Patriarch said: "The Buddha-dharma exists within the world;
it is not separate from awakening within the world. To seek Bodhi apart from the world is like seeking a rabbit's horn."
Those who wish to study the Buddha-dharma must gradually distance themselves from all things they have previously cherished;
as this is achieved, the evil karma of birth and death will likewise gradually dissolve. Such individuals are the true sons of the Buddha, whether they be laypeople or monastics.
It delivers one from all suffering and calamity.
Suffering and calamity consist of worldly fame, achievement, power, and profit; they comprise the realms of sensual desire, such as men and women, food and drink—all objects of craving.

All people greedily pursue these without satiety, thereby giving rise to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. Once obtained, there is further the suffering of losing it all. [This is] attachment...
The suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, and birth, old age, sickness, and death—all these are nothing but suffering.
All who possess a body are subject to this suffering; only those who realize the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) are not afflicted by it.

Why is this? It is because they know in advance that all things are illusory transformations. Thus, they do not rejoice when gaining them, nor do they grieve when losing them. They seek things together with others, yet they do not share their greed. With...
All things alike gain [existence], yet they do not alike perish. To dwell in the world in this manner—what suffering could there be? Therefore it is said:
"It delivers one from all suffering and calamity. Śāriputra.
The Buddha had one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples. Among them were ten great disciples, each possessing a preeminent talent;
for instance, Subhūti was foremost in understanding emptiness, while the Venerable Ānanda was foremost among the śrāvakas.
Maudgalyāyana was foremost in filial conduct; Rāhula was foremost in secret practice; and this Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom.
Whenever the Buddha preached profound sutras or teachings difficult to believe, he would summon Śāriputra to engage in dialogue and provide answers.
"Śāri" is the name of a bird in the Western Heavens; that bird’s eyesight is exceptionally swift and keen, and so was the Venerable One.
During the time he was in his mother’s womb, his mother’s wisdom and eloquence were extraordinary; the multitude immediately knew that the one she carried in her womb was a sage.
Therefore, they named his mother Śāri. When the Venerable One appeared in the world, his eloquence was peerless.
Because his mother was named Śāri, he was called Śāriputra—namely, Śāriputra. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* preached by the Buddha is indeed difficult to believe.
This is the Dharma. One may also summon them to engage in dialogue. Whether one uses the body and mind as metaphors, all such approaches are incorrect.
Form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Those of the Hīnayāna suspect that these five aggregates are substantially existent entities; because their minds are disturbed by this, they fail to attain mastery.
They must simply forget them, for only then will the mind become light and agile. All of this is due to the inverted views of sentient beings.
The Buddha spoke this section to dispel their doubts. The Buddha taught that it is not only the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) that is the nature of true emptiness;
rather, the four aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā*, *saṃjñā*, *saṃskāra*, *vijñāna*) are also of one essence with the nature of true emptiness.
He taught that these five aggregates themselves are the true nature; there is no need for selection or rejection, nor should one be confused—there is absolutely no discrimination.

Worthy One said: "The ultimate and the conventional are both extinguished, yet the two truths eternally persist. This section follows from the preceding statement that the five aggregates are all empty;

it is intended to prevent people from regarding them as substantially existent, thinking that while the five aggregates can be emptied, they must first have been real. Now, these aggregates are like a cataract: they have a name but no reality.
Change and impermanence arise and perish in succession; how could their cycles through day and night be counted?

Yet those such as the śrāvakas are afflicted by them and cannot control them, and thus they regard them as truly existent. How could they know that what is deludedly taken as an object, when transmuted, is precisely the five aggregates (pañcaskandha)?
When awakened, the transmutation of the object is itself true emptiness (śūnyatā). Because one can transmute the object, the mind does not linger upon a single thing.
Although phenomena undergo ten thousand transformations in their mutual interactions, they do not constitute a burden; therefore, it is called "true emptiness.

True emptiness is able to empty the five aggregates (*skandhas*), yet the five aggregates cannot destroy true emptiness. True emptiness is real, while the consciousness of the aggregates is illusory; the illusory depends upon the real for its existence.
The Real is not the absence of the illusory; the Real exists within the illusory, yet within the Real there is no illusion.

Students who wish to realize the nature of True Emptiness must by all means avoid loathing or detesting the five aggregates (*skandhas*). Rather, throughout the twenty-four hours of the day and night, they must examine and investigate with meticulous attention at every thought-moment.
They should observe which aggregate their current thought is currently attached to, just as one would apprehend a thief—resolutely determined to catch them.
Only when one has ceased such grasping at gain can one begin to transcend the barrier of birth and death;

only when body and mind are no longer obstructed by the five aggregates can it be called True Emptiness, and also called the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions;
therefore, I speak of the One Vehicle. Until one has realized the True Mark, one must not yet take the aggregates and consciousness to be one's true nature. Thus said the ancients.
This is what is meant by "mistaking a thief for one's son. By no means should you attempt to cast off the aggregates and consciousness in order to seek the true nature.
This is what the ancients called "fabricating a ghost. An elder monk ridiculed those who identify consciousness as the spirit, saying:

"The very root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas, the deluded person recognizes as the original true self. I shall continue his verse: "If you seek [the truth] apart from this consciousness,"
"Bodhi ultimately has no means of emerging from the six sense-objects. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi.
The Preface by Xianshou states: "It is because true emptiness is never non-existent; thus, through the existence of the illusory body, one discerns the emptiness of the real mark (dharmatā).

The illusory existence of all phenomena has, from the beginning, never been anything other than empty; thus, through this illusory emptiness of phenomena, one clarifies the true existence of the real mark."

The existence of illusory existence has form and is called "constant existence"; the existence of the true mark is without substance and is thus "empty existence. Therefore, it is said to be "not existent.

The emptiness of empty space is without substance and is called "annihilation-emptiness"; the emptiness of true emptiness has an image and is thus "existent emptiness. Therefore, it is said to be "not empty. This emptiness that is not empty is empty yet not annihilated.
The existence of that which is non-existent; existing yet not being permanent. Once the four attachments have vanished, the hundred negations are simultaneously dispelled.
This is what is meant by the profound purport of Prajñā.
"These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness.
"All" (zhū) means "many" or "multitude. "Dharmas" is the general name for all things and phenomena. This section follows from the preceding statement that form is not different from emptiness;
it says "all dharmas" because there is a concern that people might cling to a nihilistic emptiness. If this were merely an emptiness of extinction, it would certainly need to be clarified.

It is only when one brings forth the single *dharmatā* (true reality) that it is well. If one does not perceive the true reality, this is merely "annihilationist emptiness," also known as "indeterminate emptiness.

There are certain worldlings among the heterodox who possess sharp faculties; they sweep away all sensory conditions and appearances before them, yet their knowledge and vision do not transcend the realm of emptiness itself.
They then cling to this realm and take it to be the "True Emptiness. Alas! To mistake an objective realm for the Truth is not to abandon [delusion].
"What is the use of clinging to existence or non-existence? Furthermore, there was a master who, outwardly did not cling to the mark of existence and inwardly did not cling to the mark of emptiness.
He expanded his mind to encompass the entire dharma-realm, claiming that the Buddha-nature is inherently like this.
Whenever he raised an ancient kōan, he would say: "How much Buddha-nature is there? Its vast capacity pervades the dharma-realm," and so forth. Alas! Although this master knew this...
One knows the great, yet does not know the small; furthermore, one suffers from the malady of vast emptiness. Have you not heard the Buddha say:

"The great encompasses the sands of the world, while the small enters a single hair-tip"? True nature originally has no fixed measure; it is round when round, and square when square. The Sixth Patriarch said:
Its essence is identical to empty space, yet it possesses no measure of empty space.

For the most part, those whose knowledge and views fall into attachment to existence or non-existence, or who pursue notions of vastness and so forth, mostly follow after the heels of others. The Buddha once rebuked them, saying they were like "pursuing clods with a hound."

If it were a lion, it would chase after people. If a student can empty all dharmas of worldly toil, their practice will have reached the top of a hundred-foot pole, a place of extreme peril and height.
If they advance one more step, they will not fall into the bitter sea of worldly toil, but will surely fall into a vast, bottomless pit.

What the ancients called "the edge of birth and death" refers to this very point. To rejoice [in this]— [Note: The final character "忻然" (xīnrán) is left untranslated as it appears to be a concluding particle or a fragment of a phrase.]
Let go! Who dares to take this up? To advance one step further, one must have a joyful and stable dojo;
only then will there be a place to establish one’s destiny. Only then can one penetrate all religions and come to know the capacity of the student.
Only then can one cease study and end inquiry, guiding those who have not yet awakened. Should it be otherwise...
This is not so. How could one fail to pore over these ancient scrolls to seek the means of transcending the world?
For those who attain this further stage of progress, movement and stillness are tranquil; nature and form are as they are (*tathatā*). Coming and going are free; form and emptiness are unimpeded.

Cradling children and playing with grandchildren is nothing other than Buddha-work. Whether in mountain forests or in the morning markets, all places are *bodhimaṇḍas*. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The superior..."
Awakening has no place from which it comes, nor does it have any destination to which it goes. This pure and wondrous form-body manifests through the power of spiritual efficacy (*ṛddhi*).

The Sixth Patriarch said: "Is this very characteristic or is it separate from this characteristic? I replied: "Neither identical nor separate; this is precisely the true mark of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*)."
That which the Buddha calls the "empty Tathāgatagarbha" is this very thing. The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:

"There are four kinds of people who do not recognize the empty Tathāgatagarbha, like those born blind: first, ordinary worldlings; second, śrāvakas; third, pratyekabuddhas; and fourth, bodhisattvas at the initial stage.
All of these fail to recognize the emptiness of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is the true mark (*dharmatā*). Formerly, at the assembly on Mount Huangmei, the Fifth Patriarch intended to...
Regarding the verse on "Formlessness," Master Xiu said: "The body is like a Bodhi tree; once the body is understood as the tree, what then is taken to be the Bodhi?
The mind is like a bright mirror stand; once the mind is understood as the stand, what then is taken to be the mirror?
To examine the words "like" (似) and "as" (如), one already does not know one's original face; it is not merely that both body and mind are absent.
"Fallen! To place one head atop another, and furthermore to expose the two characters 'body' and 'mind'—what is this if not to cry out in grievance while clutching stolen goods?
I see Master Xiu setting up the stage, waiting for the Sixth Patriarch to come and perform the play.

Had it not been for Master Xiu, who first acted as the piece of stubborn wood, I know that even the Sixth Patriarch would have had no place to apply his axe or chisel. Having run into that fellow pounding rice, [the Patriarch]..."
He was born to seek the ultimate advantage; look at what he says—how free and easy! "Bodhi originally has no tree; one's entire body is entirely Bodhi.
How then can one distinguish anything as a tree? "The bright mirror is also not a stand;
once the mind is understood as the bright mirror, what further stand could there be? One's original face is precisely the true mark (*dharmatā*). Within this true mark, from the beginning...
"There is not a single thing; where could dust settle? Those who interpret this verse mostly offer empty conjectures. I see every word as profoundly real.
By citing these stories of the two masters, it specifically demonstrates the characteristic of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmasūnyatā*). This characteristic is inherently possessed by every person.
Each and every thing is perfectly accomplished; there is no need for laborious deliberation or contrived arrangement. It depends entirely on whether one uses it skillfully or not.
It is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
The non-extinction of thought is called "arising. Arising is but another name for non-extinction. The non-arising of discursive thoughts is called "cessation.
Cessation is merely a provisional designation for non-arising. This non-arising and non-cessation is set forth to dispel the doubts raised in the preceding passage.
It means that when the five aggregates are all empty, discursive thoughts have already ceased; once thoughts cease, the mark of emptiness immediately manifests.

[This is] understood. Only those of initial capacity are unable to see it. Fearing that they might become biased and attached to cessation—suspecting that the extinction of this thought is itself the characteristic of emptiness—the Buddha subsequently called upon Śāriputra and said: "Form is not different from emptiness.

This means that form and the other aggregates (*skandhas*) are not different from the characteristic of emptiness, in order to dispel their suspicion regarding attachment to cessation. Not only are form and emptiness non-different, he further said: "Form..."
This is emptiness. That is to say, the five aggregates are themselves true emptiness; one must not differentiate between these various aggregates.
Furthermore, fearing that students might become biasedly attached to the notion of "arising," [the text] clarifies that this very notion is the characteristic of emptiness.

Thus, at this point, both doubts are collectively dispelled, and it is said: "All these dharmas are empty. When one realizes the characteristic of emptiness, although it is not arising, it is also not...
This is cessation. This is the World-Honored One’s direct pointing to the true reality (*dharmatā*) by means of terms such as "neither arising nor ceasing.
This Dharma can only be known by the Buddha; it can only be taught by the Buddha. All the words in the various sutras are like the fingers of the Buddha;
the true nature of persons is like the bright moon in the sky. The metaphor is that the Buddha uses his finger to point at the moon for people. If a person can detach from—
Pointing at the moon means that the moon is in the sky and not on the finger. Although it is not on the finger, what is seen as the moon depends upon the pointing of the finger.

If one does not know to look away from the finger to see the moon in the sky, but instead grasps the Buddha’s finger and mistakes it for the moon, such a person not only fails to recognize the moon, but fails to recognize the finger as well. This is birth.

The three segments of the Dharma—extinction, defilement, and the increase or decrease—are like the fingers of the Buddha. By means of these fingers, he points to the nature of emptiness within the bodies of all people.
This true mark of ultimate emptiness is where the path of words is cut off in the Gate of the Patriarchs; not a single character can be established there.
Even for those who speak eloquent words, there is no opening for a word to emerge directly beneath them.
This characteristic is not something obscure, profound, difficult to know, or difficult to see; rather, it is a matter that is most simple and easy, level and straightforward.

It requires only that one realize and awaken to it oneself, without depending on the instruction of a teacher or attaining it through the Dharma. That which is attained without being caused by the Dharma is called the pearl within one's clothes.
If one obtains the Dharma through the transmission of a teacher, it is obtained by means of the śrāvaka.

The ancients said that those who enter through the gate do not possess the family treasure, because what they take is exhaustible and its use is soon depleted. Thus, the Buddha repeatedly stated in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"If I had obtained any dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Dīpaṃkara would not have [predicted my enlightenment]."
"Grant me this prediction: 'In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni.
Because there is truly no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara granted me this prediction, saying:
'In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni. Thus spoke the ancients.
To speak the single word "Zen" (Dhyāna) is to drag through mud and water; to speak the single word "Buddha" is to be filled with shame and embarrassment.
There are those of dull faculties and indolent learning who, upon hearing that the Gate of the Patriarchs does not employ words and letters, immediately sweep away all the Buddha-dharma. Alas!

It is like a person who, failing to recognize the moon, discards the finger pointing at the moon. Such people, though they pass through kalpas as numerous as grains of sand, will ultimately achieve nothing.
To recognize the moon’s timing—how tragic! Have you not heard that while the *dhāraṇī* is without words, words can manifest the *dhāraṇī*?
Non-Buddhists often divide doctrine (*śāsana*) and essence (*tattva*) into two separate segments; how could they know that doctrine serves as the vehicle for the essence?

If one establishes the essence through doctrine, yet remains mired in the essence, one fails to realize that when doctrine is transcended, there is no doctrine by which to clarify the essence. Doctrine and essence require one another; do not cling to either.
This is the supreme [teaching]. Who would say that within our tradition there is no central tenet (*zong*)? What, then, is this "mark of emptiness" (*kongxiang*) spoken of here?
It is not merely this; for all verbal explanations are explanations of a central tenet. When the Buddha spoke of "neither arising nor ceasing," he used it to point toward the mark of emptiness.
If a student realizes the tenet of the mark of emptiness, they will finally understand that "neither arising nor ceasing" is precisely the scope of the mark of emptiness.

If one understands the principle of the single aspect— that enlightenment is neither born nor extinguished— then the principles of the two aspects— the defiled and the pure, and increase and decrease—
can be known by extension across all categories.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
This section concerns the methods for those below the stage of physical form. Regarding the so-called non-existence of the six sense organs:
it does not mean that seeing and the other faculties have ceased to exist, for one can currently eat and speak; how then could the six organs be non-existent?

It is simply because ordinary people do not know that the true mind exists within themselves, and see only the sounds, forms, scents, and flavors of the world; thus their minds either follow after what the eyes perceive or...
They follow after their ears and depart; all day long they remain outside the gate, rushing about in busyness. Thus there are the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Once a practitioner of the Way has realized their emptiness, then the six faculties merge into a single faculty, and one is no longer enticed or led astray by sounds and forms. Therefore it is said:
"Thus, within the mark of emptiness, there is no burden of these six faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
There are no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects.
The eye confronts form; the ear confronts sound; the nose confronts odor; the tongue perceives taste; and the body is capable of touch.

That which constitutes the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*) refers collectively to the physical frame, the hands and feet, and the penis. "Touch" (*spraṣṭavya*) here means kicking, striking, or colliding. The faculty of the mind (*manas*) presides over...
Thought. Thought is itself the Dharma. Internally, there is deluded imagination; externally, there are phenomena and things; and all scriptural texts are likewise the Dharma.
The Dharma is the object-field (*viṣaya*) of the mental faculty (*manas*). In other contexts, it refers to the method of cultivation.
Those who possess body and mind yet do not know themselves are called *sattvas*. The nature of *sattvas* is deluded; they know only the six sense-objects external to the body. To awaken this nature—
For such a person, every thought-moment is inseparable from body and mind. Although they do not sweep or clean, their six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are pure;

thus, the sensory objects remain as objects, having no connection whatsoever with one's six sense-faculties. Therefore it is said: "Thus, within the state of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*), there is no disturbance from these six sensory objects—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena."
"There is no eye-element, and so forth, up to no consciousness-element.
This section concerns the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). The Buddha has stated this in brief; if one were to explain it in detail, one would say:
"There is no eye-element, no ear-element, no nose-element, no tongue-element, no body-element, and no mind-element. These are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Furthermore, in the formless realm, there is no realm of sound. There are no realms of the six sensory objects—odor, fragrance, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).
Nor are there the realms of the six consciousnesses. Visual consciousness and visible form constitute one realm; auditory consciousness and sound; olfactory consciousness and odor;

gustatory consciousness and taste; tactile consciousness and touch; and mental consciousness and the phenomena of thought. These faculties, objects, and consciousnesses together constitute the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). As for "realm" (*dhātu*), it means...

The boundary of boundaries is like a district; it refers to the eighteen bases (*āyatana*). Each district possesses its own specific capacity, and by means of its particular skill, they do not overlap or intermingle.
For example, the eye-faculty can only confront visible forms (*rūpa*) and has no capacity for sound.
Among the objects of the thousand forms, only those corresponding to the eye-faculty can be known by it; they cannot cause the nose to see. As for the ear-consciousness, it can only...
The consciousness-element perceives sound but cannot perceive taste. By citing these several elements, the rest may be understood by analogy.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), all are the sites where sentient beings perform their karma; they are likened to the eighteen layers of hell.

One who awakens to their true nature transforms hell into heaven and transmutes greed, anger, and delusion into precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Thus, every element is transformed into a pure land of radiant light.

Now, the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are like water and rice; the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*) are like yeast and medicinal herbs. Without yeast, water and rice will certainly not become wine;

without consciousness, the faculties and objects will certainly not produce karma. The World-Honored One teaches people to transform consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*). Wisdom is itself true emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
once consciousness is transformed into true emptiness, consciousness is already non-existent. If the faculties and objects were devoid of conscious cognition, they would be like inanimate matter.
When these are combined, the faculties remain as faculties and the objects remain as objects; how then could they subvert true emptiness? Therefore it is said:
"For this reason, within the characteristic of this emptiness, there are no dharmas of the eighteen realms."
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; and so on, up to: there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.
This dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination is identical in nature to the dharma of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

However, while the five aggregates consist of only five layers, these twelve links of dependent origination proceed from the shallow to the deep, consisting of twelve layers, beginning with ignorance. No...
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is that which drags sentient beings into hell; it is the first ghost that deludes the soul.
When an eminent person of the world attains the breaking of this ignorance, then the state of a sage or a Buddha may be expected.
As soon as even a slight emotion of joy or anger arises in the human mind, that is ignorance. If the mind does not cling to objects, from what could joy or anger arise? Indeed.
The minds of sentient beings are each and every one luminous. It is only because they have become attached to sounds and forms that this luminosity is obscured.
If a person loses such luminosity, though their eyes remain wide open, they are busily wandering as if entirely dreaming.
All manner of afflictions come forth in succession; even if one subsequently realizes it is a dream, one must shake [it off].
They toss and leap about, yet they cannot awaken; immediately thereafter, they fall back asleep. This is precisely the cause by which sentient beings enter hell.
How can ignorance not be shattered? Those who wish to shatter it must first subdue themselves, holding the sword of Prajñā-wisdom in their hands.
When sensory objects and sounds suddenly encounter one another, regardless of whether they are good or bad, one must strike with a single sword to cleave them into two pieces.

One must proceed directly until there is no longer a place to strike; only then will the net of ignorance finally shatter. Ignorance and wisdom are such that the victory of one is the defeat of the other;
they cannot coexist. If wisdom relaxes even slightly, ignorance follows immediately upon its heels. Therefore, [one must remain vigilant].
One might say that ignorance does not exist. Yet, since ignorance cannot be said not to exist, then the "exhaustion" of ignorance—even the single word "exhaustion"—can no longer be spoken of.
Since ignorance cannot be said to be exhausted, how could old age and death be said to be exhausted? Therefore it is said:
within the characteristic of emptiness, there is also no exhaustion of old age and death.
There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path.
These Four Noble Truths are metaphysical principles and serve as the vessels for those of the Mahāyāna.
Suffering and its origin are the evil causes and effects of abiding in the world; suffering is the fruit of retribution and experience, while its origin is that which creates suffering.
First, the fruit of suffering is shown so that people may know it and be afraid of it; next, the cause of accumulation is shown so that people may sever it and refrain from committing it.
This is like a household that accumulates non-virtue: this is the cause of accumulation, and there will inevitably be lingering calamity, which is the fruit of suffering.

Because one accumulates unwholesome karma, one consequently invites the suffering of further calamities. These two truths—the Cessation and the Path—are the wholesome causes and effects of the supramundane.

Cessation is the fruit of the supramundane; that which is called "attaining the fruit of cessation" means that all deluded thoughts and discursive memories are utterly cleared away so that they do not arise—this is termed "cessation.
First, the fruit of cessation is shown to inspire people’s longing for this peace and purity; next...
He demonstrates the Eightfold Noble Path to lead people toward further cultivation. As for the Eightfold Noble Path: Right Speech means that mind and mouth are in accord;

Right Action means that there is nothing that is not Buddha-work; Right Livelihood means that worldly habits have been eliminated; Right Thought means that all delusive imaginings are absent; and Right Effort [is as follows].
Not opposing the wishes of others is right mindfulness; having no other mental objects is right concentration.
When body and mind are not distracted, one is able to cultivate the causes of this Eightfold Noble Path. Then the fruit of cessation will be attained spontaneously without seeking.

This Dharma of the Four Truths is indeed simple and convenient, superior to all other dharmas. The Buddha said that for one who realizes true emptiness, the accumulation of causes is severed of its own accord.
If one is not afraid of the fruit of suffering, it will naturally vanish. When one possesses the fruit of the wisdom of Bodhi, then the fruit of cessation is no longer worth longing for.
The eighty-four thousand afflictions of the world all return to the true awakening of ultimate emptiness; what need is there to speak of the Eightfold Noble Path?
Therefore it is said: within the characteristic of emptiness, there is no dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
There is no ignorance, nor is there any attainment, because there is nothing to be attained.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, has no hindrance in his mind (and so forth), up to and including *samyaksaṃbodhi*.
Wisdom (*jñāna*) is the insight of *prajñā*. The internal delusions of sentient beings and the external afflictions all rely upon the wisdom of *prajñā* to be illuminated and shattered as illusory.
Only then can one realize the principle of the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*). Once dust-like delusions are emptied, [one attains liberation].
When the appearance of emptiness manifests, there still remains the wisdom of *prajñā* and the principle attained; because these are mixed together, it seems one has not yet reached full acuity.
These too must be gradually eliminated, so that the true mark (*dharmatā*) becomes manifest and free from confusion.
Therefore it is said: "There is neither wisdom nor attainment. When the student reaches this point, the fruits of *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi* have already been realized. Furthermore, the Buddha said:

Because there is nothing to be attained, what does a Bodhisattva do? This is likely because one fears that they might doubt whether becoming a Buddha or a Bodhisattva constitutes the fruit-stage of the Great Sages and Holy Ones;
how could it be limited merely to this "no wisdom and no attainment"? To summarize it in a single phrase:
who would not know that when all delusive thoughts and worldly afflictions are absent, one has already realized the wisdom of the emptiness of persons?
Now, having reached the stage where there is neither ignorance nor attainment, one has already attained the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
Having arrived here, one does not realize the fruit of the *pāramitās*; when, then, will this be realized?
This stage of non-attainment is not something that can be reached by ordinary means; therefore, the Buddha cites the Bodhisattvas and all the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Originally there is no cause for attaining the fruit; it is precisely because of this "non-attainment" that one attains the fruits of *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*.
This is intended to resolve the doubts of scholars and represents the World-Honored One’s earnest intent in citing scriptural evidence and entrusting the teaching.
How could those who have been moistened by the compassionate rain of the Buddha and have sprouted the roots of goodness from past lives forget their source? This non-...
Having attained its wondrous essence, students should immerse their spirits in it and study it with thorough mastery for a long time; only then will they begin to obtain its practical application.
Now, the Buddha’s discourse has already fully elucidated the *prajñā* of manifestation (*khyāta-prajñā*). Why, then, does the subsequent text further discuss the *prajñā* of secrecy (*guhya-prajñā*)?

It is because the World-Honored One, out of compassion for practitioners who have realized the principles and perfected the Dharma-illumination, [observed] that they were beset by the adverse conditions of greed, anger, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

If difficulties do not subside, and one repeatedly and knowingly creates obstacles and disturbances, causing the mind to procrastinate until reaching old age without achieving anything—all this is due to the karmic enmity of previous lives.
When these roots are firm and deep, they sprout again even after being cut away; they ruin a person’s wholesome conduct and hinder progress on the Path.
Therefore, this dharani is further taught so that people may recite it, whereby it can secretly dispel what lies before them.
...transgressions. One shall directly ascend to the shore of enlightenment. This is because the World-Honored One’s heart of loving others is inexhaustible;
therefore, he is called the Compassionate Father of the Three Realms.
Thus, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the [mantra of] no...
The above mantra is the peerless mantra; it can eliminate all suffering because it is true and not false.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā mantra is spoken. The mantra is as follows:
*gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
Generally speaking, what is called "mantra" consists of the secret words of various devas, ghost kings, and māras for commanding their respective retinues.
Now, as they would have no other offerings to present to the World-Honored One, each has brought the secret mantras used to govern their subordinates to offer to our Buddha.
If the spirits and ghosts within their retinues should disturb or harass sentient beings, one need only recite these mantras, and [the harm will cease].
All enemies and Māras will naturally retreat; such is the meaning. Why should scholars doubt this? There is no need for further explanation.
In the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*, there is a parable which says: Long ago, there was an elder whose slave fled to another country. The king of that land gave him his princess as a wife.
The slave constantly assumed an air of arrogance. When a countryman returned from his native land, he informed the elder of this.
The elder went to see the slave and welcomed him into the inner courtyard, saying to the princess, "This is my father. From that time on, the slave no longer behaved with such arrogance.
One day, when the elder wished to return home, the princess secretly told him, "Your son comes from a family of great wealth and status; it will be very difficult for you to serve him."
"I beg you to show me a single dharma. The elder said, "I have a mantra.
When you go away and people again act with arrogance toward you, you need only point one finger forward and one finger backward, making a gesture, and recite two lines of the mantra against them.
You shall travel to other lands without a companion and delude all people. If their arrogance does not cease, recite the final two lines: 'You lot!'"
"You should eat coarse food together. Why do you so frequently harbor thoughts of anger? This behavior must cease.

The princess asked for an explanation, but the elder said, "The secret words cannot be explained; simply recite them, for they possess power. When the elder returned home, the slave resumed his habitual behavior.

The Princess recited the mantra according to the ritual, and the slave’s affectations immediately ceased. The slave thought to himself, "The Elder must have informed the Princess of my background and character;
from now on, I shall no longer act with such pretension. This is generally the meaning of mantras.
As for the sounds of the mantras, they are unintelligible; they are all the *brahmā*-sounds of the devas, nāgas, and spirits. This was how the scriptures were translated at that time.
As for this scripture, why are the characters translated while the sounds are not? It is because one must chant these Sanskrit sounds to invoke divine power;

when practitioners believe in and maintain them, they will certainly obtain the effect of warding off calamities. Since we do not even dare to translate the Sanskrit sounds, how could we presume to provide further explanations of them?
Whenever I see those who attempt to explain them, they all rely on their own arbitrary conceptions to provide false annotations.
I prostrate. May those of like mind hereafter simply believe, accept, practice, and uphold this, taking it as their reliance for transcending the world;
thus, they shall not fail the compassionate intent of the World-Honored One.
Question: Regarding *nirvāṇa*, it is also called *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder). Is this death or not death?

Is it not the case that *nirvāṇa* is not attained at the moment of death? One is said to "enter *nirvāṇa*" because practitioners must eliminate deluded thoughts and the conceptualizations of sentient beings;
they must first establish *nirvāṇa* before they can transcend all such delusions. If [this were merely] dying...
If *nirvāṇa* were [merely] death, then what need would there be for the deluded thoughts [of sentient beings]? The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"I shall cause all sentient beings throughout the three realms, the nine stages, the four modes of birth, and the six paths of existence to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and thereby bring them to extinction.
If *nirvāṇa* were death, then the Buddha would have died along with all sentient beings; how could this possibly be his intention? Furthermore, it says: "The mind of *nirvāṇa* is easy to understand."
The wisdom of discernment (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*) is difficult to clarify; examine this mind of *nirvāṇa* in detail. This wisdom of discernment is not death.
One may know that this *nirvāṇa* is the very essence of the true mark of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā-tathatā*), the king among all dharmas.

When a practitioner possesses this dharma of *nirvāṇa*, then the six perfections, the myriad practices, the four truths, and the various dharmas of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* are all entirely contained therein.

This is correct. However, I fear that those whose conditions are slight, whose offenses are heavy, whose faculties are dull, or who have not long engaged in the practice, will be unable to realize the fruit suddenly.
Yet there are also those who realize it at the very moment of hearing the teaching; this depends on whether one’s doubt or faith is such as it may be. Now, there are two kinds of *nirvāṇa*.
If it is for those of the two vehicles—the *pratyekabuddhas*, the solitary awakeners (*pratyekajinas*), and the *arhats*—they understand birth and death, and they also possess *nirvāṇa*.
This is called *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) and is also termed "lesser nirvāṇa.
As for its practice, one stays far removed from clamor, renounces worldly affairs, dwells in deep seclusion and solitude, and sets one's will upon the fading away of all things.

After a long time, even all deluded thoughts and discursive reflections become still and unmoving; this is what is called nirvāṇa. Although it is called nirvāṇa, because one is still buried therein...
Below, there remain the aforementioned afflictions that have not yet been subdued; one has long guarded against sound, form, fame, and profit as enemies.
Therefore, this is called "nirvāṇa with remainder. It is like the case of [the Prince of] Yong feigning death—he ultimately could not cross the Lead Pass.

With such practice, one must absolutely refrain from attending to worldly affairs, fearing they might disturb the mind of profound stillness; thus, one guards against sound and form as if they were bandits.
An enemy. One fears human affairs as if they were shackles.
Although one may remain temporarily unmoved amidst all things—the realms of worldly toil—these are held fast by the power of meditative stillness, like young grass crushed beneath a great boulder;

though it does not sprout, the potential for growth still remains. Thus, while one may escape *nirvāṇa*, one cannot bring an end to birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, regarding birth and death...

It cannot be said that he is entirely [without fault]. Nevertheless, when compared to ordinary beings and icchantikas who drift and sink within birth and death, how could the difference between them possibly be anything less than that between heaven and earth?
Now, the Great Nirvana established by the Bodhisattvas of the eleventh stage is called "Nirvana without remainder.
Their activity consists in abiding in stillness without hastening toward it, and understanding clamor without avoiding it; they dwell within the Nirvana of profound stillness.
When one wanders through the clamorous world, the world itself is also tranquil, for there is not a single sound, form, or affliction to be avoided or feared.
When this is so, the minds of sentient beings have already been fully delivered; this is what is called ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
If even a single matter or a single object remains, such that there is the slightest lingering attachment, then that is still one sentient being.

"Not yet crossed over" is also a state of having something remaining. Only when there is not even a single thought of delusion or a notion of sentient beings to be saved is it called "without remainder.
The Buddha said: "If there were even a single sentient being who had not attained liberation, I would not have attained Buddhahood."
This is precisely the meaning. A sutra says: "The Tathāgata has realized nirvāṇa and forever severed birth-and-death. Since he has severed birth-and-death, how could there be further death?
Students should investigate and contemplate this for themselves, verifying it against the scriptures of the Buddhas; be careful not to follow others like a shadow through the world.
Bodhisattvas appear in the world at intervals, and there is no one to ask for guidance; each must prepare their own bridge and raft.
