One must not pass the days in mere complacency. A hundred-year life is but a fleeting span of time. Alas!
If this body is not saved in this present life, in what other life shall one save it? Be careful, be careful!
Question: What is meant by "true emptiness" (*śūnyatā*), and why is it also called the "real mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the "mark of emptiness," and the "true nature" (*tathatā*)?
Are these one or two? Answer:
To speak in detail, they are called true emptiness and the real mark; to speak briefly, they are called the mark of emptiness. In sum, they are all the primordial reality.
This is another name for *xing* (nature). The physical form of the body is the vessel that carries the Way. Without the body, the mind has no support; without the mind, the body has no master.
Since the mind is the master of the body, it is called *xing*. Because the body possesses the mind as its master, it is substantial; thus it is termed the "true mark" (*shixiang*).
In Buddhist scriptures, the character for *xing* refers to the mind as the master being the nature; this was specifically preserved by the translators.
This is the meaning. If the body were without the mind to preside over it, it would be empty. Being empty, it is called an illusory appearance; it is also called a deluded body.
When the mind relies upon the body, it naturally casts off all delusions of sound, form, fame, and profit;

thus, the mind is simply empty. When the mind is empty, there is no longer any illusion or falsehood to intermingle with it; therefore, it is called "true emptiness. That the mind is empty is not merely...
The mind is true. When the mind is empty, the body is non-active and at ease, entirely free from entanglements. In this state, the body, too, is empty.
When both body and mind are empty, yet there still exist a body and mind that can be pointed out as real, what else could this be but the nature of the true emptiness and true mark?
The followers of the Two Vehicles discard and eliminate body and mind, yet they remain attached to the realm of the view of emptiness; how can they be compared to true emptiness?
They speak of the same thing.

Now, as for this physical body composed of the four great elements, it exists in its present formation and requires no further adjustment. It is only the mind that is difficult to see and difficult to awaken to;
because the mind is not awakened, delusive thoughts swarm together. Therefore, all the Dharma gates taught by the Buddha are nothing more than instructions for people.
When one clarifies their original mind, habitual tendencies and deluded karma naturally vanish, and the Tathāgatagarbha immediately manifests;

there is no need to perform any ascetic practices, and one may likewise be liberated from the suffering and calamities of birth and death. How great is the Buddha’s grace—how could the vastness of heaven serve as an adequate metaphor?

Yet, how is it that the Buddha’s grace is seen to be so great? It is because the Buddha attained the Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which was not something achieved within this present life.

And it was thus attained. All of this was due to the fact that throughout tens of millions of kalpas in previous eons, one practiced and tested every single dharma-gate, whether great or small, until one finally realized that this Dharma of True Reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is the king among all dharmas.
Those later students who obtain this Dharma need not perform any ascetic practices at all. Reflect on this quietly: for our sakes, the Buddha...

Future generations of Buddha-sons will thus save themselves much effort and exchange it for a vast reduction of the sufferings of birth and death. Those who attain this should recognize the toil and hardship involved;
only then can they be said to repay the Buddha’s kindness. It is like casting one's body to a starving tiger or cutting off one's own flesh to feed a hawk.
Sacrificing one's body by having it dismembered limb by limb, or giving up one’s life to exchange for half a verse—these are all examples of ascetic practices.

The Buddha cultivated various forms of asceticism in order to seek the Dharma that transcends the world. Now that we have obtained the Dharma King of True Reality, we must certainly contemplate its source.
An ancient master said: "To offer this body and mind to every dust mote and land—that is what is called repaying [the Buddha's kindness]."

The Buddha’s kindness! Those who do not contemplate the Buddha’s kindness are not true children of the Buddha. For later students to encounter this Dharma-gate of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is like a one-eyed turtle encountering the hole in a floating log.
Why is this? Because there are three difficulties: it is difficult to obtain a human body; [it is difficult to hear the Dharma]; and [it is difficult to meet a Buddha].
It is difficult to be born in the Central Land, and it is difficult to encounter the Buddha-dharma. All those who possess blood and breath have a body;
why then is it said that a human body alone is difficult to obtain? It is because the human body is of the same category as the Buddha, and the Buddha-dharma exists within the human realm;
one must first obtain a human body before one can hear the teachings on transcending the world. I often observe those who lack the karmic affinity with the Buddha—ten thousand...

If one does not hear the name of the Buddha for an entire kalpa, by what means could one possibly hear his Dharma beforehand? Having already obtained a human body, it is further necessary to be born in a central land (*madhyadeśa*).
If one is born in a remote borderland or among the lowly and base, there will be no Buddha-Dharma to be heard; therefore, it is said that birth in the Central Land is difficult.
Even if one should happen to be born there, one is mostly entangled by worldly conditions, passing through a lifetime in a state of constant bustle and distraction. There is...
One may have the leisure to hear the Buddha-dharma, yet one may also lack the intention to go and hear the Buddha-dharma; therefore, it is said that the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter.
Once the Buddha-dharma has been heard, the ocean of Dharma is boundless. To briefly describe its gateways, there are likewise eighty-four thousand.

Yet this gateway of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the most difficult to encounter even among those things that are difficult to encounter. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If there should be someone who hears [this]..."
When one has pure faith in this sutra, the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) immediately arises. You should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
Between heaven and earth, only humans are noble; among those born as humans, body and mind are paramount.
Joy and sorrow, pain and itching, are interrelated within and without; indeed, nothing is more intimate than this. Yet worldly people do not realize this.

How noble! All these things—merit, fame, profit, and desire—are but false constructs that, in turn, burden the person. One busies oneself and rushes about, seeking all day long without rest at any time.
It is for this reason of this great matter (mahā-kṛtya), that the World-Honored One appeared in the world.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, he preached various sublime Dharmas to cause them to turn away from the heterodox and return to the orthodox, to reject the false and follow the true.

He truly sought to make them understand that the body is the precious vessel for the mind, and the mind is the treasure that nourishes the body; once this human form is lost, it is difficult to regain even in ten thousand kalpas.
As the days and months pass by, though one may regret it later, can one ever truly turn back? Yet those of the Buddhist tradition today regard this body as a mere excrescence or a tumor.
"What is it? It is that skin-sack. He sang of it thus: 'This skin-sack is full of obstructions; it brings total harm to my spiritual mind (lingtai).
With every step and every movement it devises schemes, and from left and right it teaches me that I am not free.
It demands food to eat, clothes to wear, and further craves glory and the ways of the world, causing my heart to be startled without a moment's respite. For your sake, it has bound me down.'"
What a grievous debt! Who would have known that this song by the Sixth Patriarch was intended to resolve the doubts of sentient beings who cling to their bodies and fear death?
He expounded this dharma of breaking through appearances to warn people to abandon this impermanent body and world, and to strive to preserve the eternally abiding true mind.

Because they do not awaken to the source of the Patriarch’s intent, this skin-sack is truly loathsome. Consequently, there are those who throw themselves from cliffs, rush into flames, wade through water, or face the blade—treating their lives as lightly as worn-out sandals.
Their intention is that if this illusory body did not exist, they would be free from the burdens of food, clothing, cold, and heat;
yet they fail to realize that if one dies with the ground of the mind (cittabhūmi) unenlightened, there remains much more upon that very mind.
Deluded thoughts and emotional consciousness have not yet been resolved; thus, one must again emerge from and enter into shells, returning once more to the human world among the four modes of birth.

To resolve these deluded notions, try observing them with the eye of wisdom: these people seek only the fame of high status and nobility, failing to take wise teachers or virtuous friends as their guides, until their corruption reaches this point.
Furthermore, they do not reflect that the end of the song says: "Urine and excrement channels, pus and blood."
This collection, when calculated, possesses what trace of elegance? The nine apertures are all pits of impurity; the six gates are entirely doorways of disorder.
When one attains understanding within this semblance of a body, the skin-sack transforms into a marketplace for radiant pearls. Sever the mind of desire; it must be firm and steadfast.
Consider that my body was born from craving and lust; once the mind of desire is severed, there is no coming or going. Within, there remains but a single [jewel].

The great luminous pearl shines with radiance day and night, naturally illuminating one’s path. This is like the Sixth Patriarch transforming the great earth into gold and churning the long river into cream and curd;
he took the four elements to construct a "transformed city. Whether a traveler is deluded or awakened depends entirely upon themselves.
What the Buddhist tradition calls the "transcendental dharma" is nothing other than this: it simply means that every person can become a Buddha. Therefore—
That which is unwholesome arises entirely from the three faculties of body, speech, and mind, which are constantly defiled by the three karmas of greed, anger, and delusion.
When these three karmas are divided, they constitute the ten unwholesome paths of action (*daśākuśala*). Specifically, the bodily faculty has three karmas:
killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. The mental faculty has three karmas: greed, anger, and delusion. The vocal faculty has four karmas: frivolous speech, lying, and malicious slander.

To indulge in these ten evils is to sow for oneself the causes of rebirth in hell. If one can transform the ten evils into the ten virtues, then when their retribution is exhausted, they will certainly be born in heaven.
How can one not be cautious? There are some members of the monastic community who have thoroughly mastered both the fundamental principle and the teachings.
They recognize cause and understand effect, and they are clever and capable; yet outwardly they practice monastic decorum while inwardly they remain as worldly as ever.

These ten evil deeds they commit again and again despite their repentance, with no end in sight. They claim that by relying on the power of the Buddha, these acts will surely be extinguished for them.

When the retribution of calamity finally descends upon one's person, one can only lament that the Buddha lacks spiritual efficacy. Alas! Have you not heard that even the Buddha’s own hand cannot shield one from karmic retribution?
The essential point lies in the individual confessing their past transgressions before Him and repenting so as to ensure they are never committed again in the future.
In this way, the fruit of Buddhahood may indeed be hoped for.
There are teachers who have mastered a single treatise on phonology; those who can perform a ritual feast for hungry ghosts (*yankou*);
those who can recall several koans; those who understand several volumes of sutra commentaries; and those who can seize and stabilize their thoughts so they do not move. Each of these...

Claiming for themselves that they had attained the essential Dharma of the Chan school and grasped the definitive intent of Bodhidharma’s "not establishing words and letters," they swept away all Buddhist teachings as blind delusions and ignorance, thereby increasing their arrogance.
They also emulated veteran masters by brandishing their staffs and raising their fly-whisks.
Assuming artificial airs and postures, they peddle gāthās; forming cliques and factions, they establish their own sectarian walls.
With no one before their eyes, they act as if Śākyamuni had been reborn. Yet within these ten directions, their pursuit of fame, profit, and the self-other duality remains rooted in worldly karma.
Such is their conduct that it is a misfortune for the Dharma gate. Consequently, they were exposed by the donors, who came to despise them as if they were mere beasts. This was the end.
He has damaged his own roots of goodness, undermined the faith of others, and ruined the pure regulations of the Buddha; this is truly lamentable.

Since the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa more than four thousand years ago, the teachings of the Elephant Vehicle have reached the height of decline. While those of the Śākya lineage are indeed many, the followers of Pāpīyān are no fewer.

To seek among them those who are free from greed and envy is truly like searching for gold in the sand. May all virtuous believers of the ten directions be careful not to look upon the faults of others.
This obstructs one's own future prospects. Although the precepts and conduct of such people may be deficient, they are still called sons of the Buddha.

Since they revere Buddhas carved from clay or wood, as well as sutras printed on paper or written with brushes—these being specifically the Two Jewels—they must also have the Sangha Jewel, which necessarily requires human beings to constitute it, so as to complete the Three Jewels abiding in the world. These Three Jewels are the merit of all the faithful.
The field [of merit] is the fertile soil for planting wisdom; it cannot be compared to the merit of repairing bridges or leveling roads.
To revere the Triple Gem brings inexhaustible rewards. Nowadays, people know only to respect the Buddha and the sutras, yet they treat ordinary monks with contempt.
Is this not a deficiency in one's own cultivation of the field of merit? Even as for ordinary monks, they should not be rejected or cast aside, nor...
One might as well say that there are no people at all. The Sixth Patriarch said: "He is not wrong, and I am not wrong. He also said:
"If you see the faults of others, your own fault lies to your left. A popular proverb says: "A monk comes to look upon the Buddha’s face.

Even if he is impure, he is still my field of merit; how could I abandon him? An ancient saying goes: "By honoring an illusory monk, one causes a true monk to preach the Dharma; by bowing to clay [statues], one encounters the living Buddha."
The Dragon. Moved by the true dragon’s bringing of rain, the Sūtra says: "If one wishes to repay the kindness of the white crow, one must provide food for the black crows.
I send word to my fellow dharma-kinsmen: subdue your present arrogance. Since you have left the household life, your minds should be free from desire;

if you cultivate the precepts with rigorous purity, who would not revere you? If even a single thought is not distracted, the five fragrances will naturally waft forth. Step back one move, and you will find your footing.
Be at ease with yourself. This is the family tradition of the Buddha’s heirs: it should be simple and plain. Beyond the concerns of hunger and cold, you should have no other thoughts.
If you can truly abide in such contentment, you will likely benefit both yourself and others.
Question: Does the Buddhist tradition also maintain the continuity of human relations?

Answer: Buddhism is called the "transcendent dharma" (lokottara-dharma); it departs from the secular world and focuses its efforts on the preservation of the mind. For this reason, it cannot simultaneously sustain the social norms and constants (gangchang).
It willingly accepts the censure of being a heterodox teaching, for it is not that they do not wish to perfect their own influence, but rather that it is impossible to maintain both.
It is so. Recently, there have been heterodox practitioners who falsely claimed that Śākyamuni also continued the human lineage, with Yaśodharā as his wife and Rāhula as his son.
Those in later generations who assert that the Śākya lineage severed its ancestral ties and continued them [in this manner] have all lost the true transmission.
I shall attempt to cite one or two major points for debate; from these, their deceptions can be understood by extension. Since the Buddha valued human relations, he must surely have had sons.
Why did Rāhula, having married, don the black robes and shave his head, abandoning his royal lineage to become the foremost monk? This is the first point that cannot be trusted.
As the Buddha was the founder of the teaching, his robe and bowl were personally transmitted to Kāśyapa; this succession of transmission serves as a model for ten thousand generations.
One must establish a household to cultivate the four occupations. Why then allow those with shaven heads and square robes to attend upon the Buddha’s seat alone for their entire lives?
These two [categories] are not to be trusted. Although the assembly of the Buddha includes many devas and humans, they do not exceed the fourfold community:
men who have shaved their hair and left home without wives are called *bhikṣus*; women who have shaved their hair and left home without husbands are named *bhikṣuṇīs*.
A lay disciple who has a wife and retains his hair is called an *upāsaka*; a female disciple who has a husband and retains her hair is called an *upāsikā*.
This clearly distinguishes between the monastic and the laity, as well as between the clergy and the laity. How can a blind master dare to offer such reckless criticisms?
This is the third point that is unworthy of belief. Furthermore, I observe that he plunders the Daoist school, [misappropriating] their practice of "controlling the qi with the spirit."

Regarding "artful methods" (*quan shu*): this refers to those who take the Taiji and the *Hé tú* as their guiding principles. They visualize a hollow sphere within the spinal column, calling it "turning the back to the mountain" (*gèn bèi*).

They circulate the breath at the navel center, naming it "walking the courtyard" (*xíng tíng*). Taking the Buddhist principle that "the myriad dharmas return to one" to mean they return to this single vital energy (*qì*), they force various religious tenets into their practice of circulating the breath.
These heterodox schools falsely claim greatness and self-importance, with their masters styling themselves as teachers of the Three Teachings; this is not [the true path].

To claim that Confucianism is drawn into Buddhism is clearly a heterodox path that deludes people like a wild fox; it is well known that such a thing cannot possibly please the lions and elephants of the monastic community.
A solitary firefly, failing to measure its own worth, first flaunts itself in a desire to equal the hare and the crow.
Let those of later generations not fall into the pit of this folly, but each exert yourselves with vigorous self-reflection and awakening.

Postscript to the Explanation of Doubts Concerning the Heart Sūtra.

During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the Śramaṇa Xuanzang was sent to the Western Regions to retrieve the scriptures. Upon reaching the kingdom of Kaśmīra, the road was perilous and infested with tigers and leopards.

The malevolent spirits were powerless to do anything. Suddenly, he saw a monk with a body covered in sores and a filthy appearance, who orally transmitted to him one scroll of the *Heart Sūtra* and commanded Xuanzang to recite it.
Thereupon, the mountains and rivers became level and open, the roads naturally cleared, tigers and leopards hid their forms, and demons and spirits vanished from sight.
This is the origin of this *Heart Sūtra*; the power of the Prajñā mantra is vast and sublime, capable of delivering [beings].
"All suffering" is clearly and sufficiently proven by this. I have long cherished this sutra; its phrasing is concise and its meaning is profound.

As I recite it aloud and contemplate it in my mind, I am lost in a vast expanse, unable to discern its boundaries or find its source. Thus, I have exhaustively consulted the commentaries of various masters to study it.
The more I studied, the more obscure it became, and the more my doubts increased. I felt ashamed of my own dull and dark nature, wandering about in a state of restless anxiety.

In the year of Yiyou (1745), I was fortunate enough to meet Master Xie Mo-hu of Yanping. He was sincere and unadorned, entirely free from the sense of self and others; he was one who had plumbed the depths of Chan.
We halted our carriage and conversed, gazing at one another; yet I was unable to press him for further instruction. The Master had already entered the chamber of the Mind-Teaching (Xinxue).
I then knelt down and asked him to resolve my doubts, saying: "Students frequently recite the Heart Sutra, yet they do not understand its meaning; they merely recite it according to the text.
I pray that you, Master, will give rise to the Bodhicitta and explain it for those of dull faculties. The Master said: "You say you rely on..."
I recite and contemplate the text, yet I fear the meaning remains unclear; upon what basis should one recite it? Furthermore, all sūtras spoken by the World-Honored One begin with "Thus have I heard.
How does this sūtra differ? I replied, "It begins with 'Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. The Master smiled broadly and said, "You are mistaken from the very first word you open your mouth.
This is a foolish error based on a single insight; please allow me to correct you. Now, this sūtra consists of two hundred [verses]..."
These sixty characters encompass the wondrous meanings within the entire Tripiṭaka.

Chanting the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, students must wholeheartedly contemplate and realize, word by word and phrase by phrase, the essential secret of the World-Honored One’s transmission of the mind-seal—the gateway for transcending birth and death.
Since it exclusively elucidates Prajñā as its primary tenet, the three characters "Avalokiteśvara" are established as a single phrase and placed at the beginning of the sūtra.
First: that *prajñā* is precisely this wisdom (*jñāna*). Wisdom is observation (*vipaśyanā*). That which is capable of observing is the Way of the true mark of ultimate emptiness;
it does not reside in the scriptural text, but within the square inch of the heart. Why should liberation (*svatantra*) be unattainable?
Why should suffering and calamity be impossible to transcend? The ancients said that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the backbone of the Great Canon.
The *Essence* (Marrow) is what the ignorant call the *Heart Sūtra*; it is, moreover, the very lifeblood of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

For your sake, I shall expand upon the meaning of the sūtra, gathering together what has been heard from predecessors while occasionally interjecting my own insights; this I shall name "Explanation of the Meaning" (*Shiyi*).

Furthermore, I shall extract those points that are doubtful and present them in sequence; this I shall name "Resolution of Doubts" (*Shiyi*). If you can follow the logic of the text, reciting it with your mouth and practicing it with your mind, then within your breast—

Long-standing knots were suddenly untied; from that moment on, he attained sudden enlightenment and first realized that the aggregates and consciousness are themselves True Suchness (*tathatā*), and that True Suchness is not external to the nature of consciousness.
Alas! The Patriarch Śākyamuni said: "This body of the five aggregates takes consciousness as its root; consciousness is the source of all delusions."
It cannot be turned away by the twelve links of dependent origination, the eighteen realms, the four noble truths, or any other phenomena.

Only those who possess the profound wisdom of *prajñā*—whose enlightened essence is perfectly luminous and who can thus understand clearly for themselves—can do so. Therefore it is said: "Learning the Dharma for a thousand days is not equal to learning *prajñā* for a single day.
Through this single gateway of *prajñā*, all phenomena are subsumed; for this reason, the sutras specifically point to *prajñā* as encompassing all dharmas.
All phenomena are said to be non-existent; only this Prajñā is the king among all dharmas.
The Bodhisattvas of the eleven stages rely upon it to realize nirvāṇa, and the Buddhas of the three periods of time rely upon it to attain perfect enlightenment.
For those in future generations who wish to cross to the other shore of bodhi, how could they abandon the boat and oars of Prajñā? Therefore, the name of this sūtra is *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom. Having received the sublime instructions of my teacher, I kneel to recite it morning and evening without ceasing.
